analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 15 or more workers to provide at least seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by Senator Kennedy with 15 Democratic cosponsors, read twice, placed on the Senate calendar, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require most employers with 15 or more employees to give workers at least seven paid sick days a year, with a prorated amount for part-time workers. Workers could use the days for their own illness or medical care, or to care for a sick child, spouse, parent, or similar family member. It also barred employers from firing or penalizing workers for using the leave, set up Labor Department enforcement, and directed a government study of costs and benefits. The bill never moved past being placed on the Senate calendar.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who currently get no paid sick leave, or leave they cannot use to care for family members. The bill's own findings note that 76 percent of the poorest families lack regular sick leave, that many workers cannot use leave for a sick child, and that the burden falls hardest on low-wage workers, especially women who handle most family caregiving.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without paid sick leave, especially low-wage workers

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 15 or more employees must provide at least seven paid sick days annually for full-time workers and a prorated amount for those working at least 20 hours a week or 1,000 hours a year.
Leave can be used for the worker's own illness or medical care, preventive care, or to care for a child, spouse, parent, or a person with a family-like relationship.
It is unlawful to fire or discriminate against a worker for using or requesting sick leave, and taking leave cannot count against a worker under no-fault attendance policies.
The bill directs a Comptroller General study of costs and benefits to employers and employees, including effects on retention, emergency room use, and children sent to school sick.
Employers with more generous existing policies need not change them, and no employer may cut existing leave to comply, so the bill sets a floor rather than a ceiling.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees, who would pay wages for the leave days and administrative costs for recordkeeping, notices, and medical certification. Businesses near the 15-employee threshold face the largest relative cost increase, since the mandate applies in full at that size.
analysis.who_pays_short: Covered employers, especially those near the 15-employee threshold

drawbacks.text: Paid leave is a direct cost to employers, and the bill requires businesses with as few as 15 employees to provide the full seven days, which falls proportionally hardest on small firms near that threshold.

The bill requires employers to keep compliance records, post notices, and manage medical certification for leaves longer than three days, adding administrative work; a willful posting violation carries a fine of up to $100 per offense.

Workers without a regular health care provider could have trouble obtaining the certification the bill allows employers to require for longer absences; the bill recognizes this and directs regulators to specify how such workers certify a leave, but leaves the solution to rulemaking.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, seven paid sick days can mean the difference between seeing a doctor and losing a day's pay or a job, and the bill's findings tie sick leave to lower infection spread and lower emergency care costs. The offsetting cost is real and falls on employers, with the sharpest pinch on the smallest covered firms, and the certification rules add friction. The bill attempts to limit both problems, by crediting existing generous policies, barring cuts to current leave, and letting regulators tailor certification for workers without insurance. On balance it is a straightforward wage-and-benefit floor with moderate, predictable compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but no committee took it up and no senator ever brought it to a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the Healthy Families Act on May 19, 2005, joined by 14 other Democratic senators as cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and placed it on the legislative calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 111, on May 20, 2005.
No further action appears in the record: no committee referral, hearing, markup, or floor vote occurred in the remaining life of the 109th Congress.
Congress adjourned on January 3, 2007, and the bill died on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with 15 or more workers, especially those that provide no paid sick leave, are better off because the mandate never came. Workers who lack paid sick days gained nothing, and a version of this idea would not become law for years.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that provide no paid sick leave

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: 14 Democratic senators
for.role: Cosponsors (Durbin, Mikulski, Murray, Harkin, Dodd, Lautenberg, Corzine, Akaka, Boxer, Feingold, Schumer, Dayton and others)

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate floor and calendar in the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor action after it was placed on the calendar, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported it; Republicans held the Senate majority and controlled whether bills reached the floor.

industries.industry: Employers with 15 or more employees (retail, food service, hospitality, and other low-benefit sectors)
industries.note: These employers would pay for the seven sick days and handle the compliance paperwork; the industries with the fewest workers already getting paid leave would bear the biggest adjustment. Workers in those sectors are the ones who gain the leave.

industries.industry: Businesses that already offer equivalent paid leave
industries.note: The bill credits existing policies that are at least as generous and bars cutting current leave to comply, so firms with good leave policies face little change beyond posting notices.
